01 What Happened
Act I
R1–5 · Ford's Half
Ford came in sharp — southpaw counters, timing, a persistent right hand. R1 produced the night's strangest moment: Foster threw Ford through the ropes after a missed jab. Stern warning, no deduction. But Foster was already doing something in those early rounds that the scorecards don't capture cleanly: gathering information. Left foot outside Ford's right foot — classic orthodox vs. southpaw positioning — already established. The rounds were close. Foster was downloading.
Act II
R6–10 · Foster Finds It
By R6 Foster had found his rhythm. Ford's output dropped — throwing one punch at a time by R7, showing fatigue. Foster moved to high guard, catch-and-counter. Volume, jab control, body work. Ford still had flashes — stepped it up in R10 — but Foster was controlling the action and scoring more. The broadcast had it close. It was close. But Foster had taken the middle of the fight.
Act III
R11–12 · No Doubt
Foster closed it cleanly. R11 and R12 were his clearest rounds of the night — body work, combinations, no question who was winning. Those two rounds probably won him the fight. One judge still had it a draw. The other two had it Foster. Majority decision. WBC retained. The crowd in Houston had their answer.
Foster landing in the championship rounds · Credit: Zachariah Delgado/Matchroom Boxing

The fight was genuinely close throughout. Ford is not a stepping stone — he came in with a plan and pushed a WBC champion the distance. The 114-114 draw card from Migliore wasn't an outrage. But Foster's footwork advantage was present from round one. The early rounds were competitive — close enough that reasonable scorecards could go either way — but Foster was never lost. He was reading. By R6 he had what he needed: high guard, catch-and-counter, body work. A champion who can absorb a competitive first half and then impose his will in the second is a different animal than one who needs a clean start to win.

Seven punches separated them across twelve rounds. Twenty percent connect rate for both. The CompuBox is exactly what the scorecards said it was: a genuinely tight fight where the winner was determined by who controlled the pace in the rounds that mattered most.

03 After The Bell
Foster and Shakur Stevenson · Post-fight confrontation · Fertitta Center

Shakur Stevenson was at ringside. The program called it. What the program didn't fully anticipate was the theater that followed. Foster called Shakur out from the ring. Shakur didn't wait — he climbed through the ropes, got in Foster's face, called him a bum in front of the Houston crowd. Security separated them. Foster: "I told you I was gonna beat your son."

Blotter Editorial — The Shakur Question
Foster didn't do enough Saturday night to make a legitimate case for the Shakur fight. The emotion in that ring was real. The desire is real. But Shakur Stevenson is No. 4 on this P4P list for a reason — he is too polished, and he is getting better. A majority decision over Raymond Ford, however gritty, does not move that needle. Foster is a very good fighter. Shakur is operating at a different level.
Foster retains the WBC super featherweight title · Houston · May 30, 2026

Charlie Sheehy TKO9 Nike Theran
Super Lightweight · TKO · Round 9
Theran replaced Jared Quiroz on less than a week's notice — the Blotter had the right opponent in the program but missed the late substitution. Context matters for evaluating the finish. That said, Sheehy looked genuinely good against a late-replacement opponent who accepted on short notice: speed, accuracy, levels, body work that set up the TKO. Performance grades higher than the opponent quality on paper. The source gap: Tapology posts opponent changes within hours. Day-of verification check is being added to the production protocol.

Omari Jones UD8 Diego Zuniga
Lightweight · Unanimous Decision · 80-71 × 3 · Prospect Watch No. 7
Zuniga replaced Alan Sanchez on short notice — Sanchez would have been the real test for an Olympic bronze medalist. Jones dropped Zuniga in R1 with the left hand, hurt him again in R7 with the same punch, but never committed to the finish. Throwing one punch at a time throughout. Not going to the body — headhunting. The left hand is clearly the weapon. He's not using it. Against Sanchez this approach doesn't work. The prospect watch entry stays, but this was a concerning performance against a lesser test. Next fight tells us something.

06 Call Audit
✓
Direction — Foster wins. Correct. Foster by majority decision, WBC retained.
✓
Method — Decision. Correct. The program's sharpest specific call in Vol. I: "the method was always a decision" and "it does not produce a stoppage against a man who has never been stopped." Ford had never been stopped. The method was a decision. Both confirmed.
✓
Shakur watching. Correct — and then some. The program flagged Shakur would be ringside. He didn't just watch. He climbed through the ropes.
✓
Fight management. The program correctly identified Foster as the superior tactician. The early rounds were close and competitive — not a Ford takeover. Foster was gathering information. The adjustment came by R6. That is exactly what the program described.
Protocol Update — Day-Of Verification
The Sheehy-Theran opponent substitution was missed. The Blotter had the right opponent in the program but didn't catch that Theran replaced Quiroz on less than a week's notice. Fix: Tapology's event pages and promoter social accounts post changes within hours. A Day-Of Verification check — within 24 hours of fight night — is now standing protocol. Being added to Blueprint v3.10 as a mandatory production step.
07 Program Grade
Vol. I · No. 16 · Foster-Ford · Final Grade
A-
Direction right. Method exactly right — the most specific and accurate call in Vol. I to date. Shakur subplot predicted and delivered beyond expectations. The early rounds were close and competitive, not a Ford takeover — Foster was reading and adjusting, exactly as the program described. Three calls, three confirmed. The method call — a decision, specifically, because Ford had never been stopped — remains the sharpest single prediction in Vol. I. That's not a guess. That's analysis.
